v: Calgary's first oil boom started with a gas well.
In nineteen-eleven, a rancher named William Herron noticed gas seeping out along the Sheep River.
He teamed up with a driller, Archibald Dingman, and some of Calgary's most influential businessmen. In nineteen-thirteen, they started drilling in Turner Valley, southwest of the city.
On May fourteenth, nineteen-fourteen, a well in Turner Valley, Dingman Number One, blew in.
Calgary went wild. People drove out to see it, and filled their cars straight from the well.
More than five hundred oil companies were started. Some brokers were so swamped with orders, they locked their doors.
The Calgary Herald reported more than four hundred thousand dollars pulled from savings accounts at Calgary banks.
But it wasn't the oil investors had hoped for. The well had struck wet natural gas, rich in a light liquid called naphtha.
That August, the First World War began, and the boom was over.
By the end of the war, all but twenty-one of those companies had failed. Most never even drilled a well.
In nineteen twenty-one, Imperial Oil took over Dingman's company. Alberta's energy history archive says that confirmed Calgary as the centre of Canada's oil and gas industry.
Turner Valley kept going. In nineteen twenty-four, Royalite Number Four erupted in fire, at a place called Hell's Half Acre.
Turner Valley flared away about ninety percent of its gas supply.
Then in nineteen thirty-six, a well called Royalties Number One struck oil, and set off another oil boom.
According to Calgary Economic Development, Calgary today is home to head offices of almost every major company in the energy business.
So, did you know Calgary's first oil boom started with gas?
